message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This bid is unusual in that it is not based on assumptions about demand: we tested the exact opening pattern at Ashgrove before asking for a penny, and measured the results hour by hour. The pilot showed strong uptake, with evening visits running close to daytime levels and Sunday sessions very popular with families, and new memberships up by about two-thirds on the year before. That gives Members real local evidence that the hours will be used. The costing is equally careful. Staffing is built up from first principles, hours times staff times weeks times branches at the correct graded rate with on-costs, and utilities are taken from actual pilot spend rather than estimates, all of which sums to £174,000. We also looked seriously at the cheaper self-service alternative and explain why it would cost more once building works are included. I am confident this is a well-tested, carefully costed proposal that delivers on the Council Plan.
</author>

<document>
Budget Justification: Extended Opening Hours at Five Branch Libraries, 2027-28
Library Services, Westmoor Borough Council, September 2026

1. Request
Library Services requests a growth bid of £174,000 in the 2027-28 revenue budget to extend opening hours at five branch libraries (Ashgrove, Fenwick, Holt Lane, Kingsmead and Millbrook) by ten hours a week each, from 38 to 48 hours.

2. Rationale
The five branches currently close at 5 pm on weekdays and do not open on Sundays. Residents' surveys have repeatedly identified opening hours as the main barrier to library use among working-age adults: in the 2025 Residents' Survey, 44% of non-users aged 25-54 said the library "is never open when I can go". The Council Plan commits to increasing library use among working-age residents and to supporting adult learning and job-seeking.

Each branch would add late opening until 8 pm on Tuesdays and Thursdays (six additional hours) and Sunday opening from 11 am to 3 pm (four additional hours).

3. Evidence from the Ashgrove pilot
From October 2025 to March 2026, Ashgrove trialled exactly this pattern, funded from one-off underspends.

Table 1. Ashgrove pilot: average visits per opening hour, October 2025 to March 2026
Time slot | Visits per hour
Weekday 9 am - 12 pm | 46
Weekday 12 pm - 5 pm | 58
Tuesday and Thursday 5 pm - 8 pm (new) | 21
Saturday 9 am - 1 pm | 64
Sunday 11 am - 3 pm (new) | 52

Over the pilot, Ashgrove recorded 1,140 new library memberships, compared with 690 in the same months a year earlier. Sunday sessions were particularly popular with families, and a weekly job club in the Thursday evening slot was fully booked from its third week.

Evening visits at Ashgrove averaged close to the weekday daytime level, which shows that there is strong latent demand for evening opening and that the new hours will be well used across all five branches.

4. Costs
Additional hours need two staff on duty at all times, in line with the Council's lone-working policy. Staffing is calculated on 50 weeks a year, allowing for bank holiday closures.

Table 2. Cost of extended hours, five branches
Item | Basis | Cost
Staffing | 10 hours x 2 staff x 50 weeks x 5 branches = 5,000 hours at £24.80 per hour (including on-costs) | £124,000
Utilities and caretaking | £6,500 per branch | £32,500
Self-service kiosk upgrades (maintenance contract) | 5 branches | £7,500
Total | | £174,000

The staffing rate is the mid-point of the Library Assistant grade plus 28% on-costs and an enhancement for Sunday working. Utilities and caretaking costs are based on the actual additional costs recorded at Ashgrove during the pilot, scaled to a full year.

5. Value for money
At current visit rates, the extra hours across the five branches would generate roughly 84,000 additional visits a year, at a cost of around £2 per visit. This compares favourably with the borough's average cost per library visit of £3.40.

6. Alternatives considered
We considered opening the branches with self-service access only in the extra hours, as some authorities have done. This would cut staffing costs by around two-thirds, but the Council's insurers have advised that unstaffed opening would require building alterations and CCTV at an estimated £60,000 per branch, and it would not support the job club and family activities that drove much of the pilot's success.

7. Risks
Recruitment. We expect to fill most additional hours from existing part-time staff who have asked for more hours, as happened during the pilot.
Demand at other branches. Ashgrove is our busiest branch, and demand at the other four may be lower. We will review usage after six months.

8. Conclusion
The twelve-month Ashgrove pilot has demonstrated strong demand for evening and Sunday opening, with new memberships up by two-thirds and evening use close to daytime levels. We ask Members to approve a growth bid of £174,000 to extend this successful model to all five branches from April 2027.
</document>
response:
# Review: Extended Opening Hours Budget Justification

**Verdict:** A pilot-based bid is a good approach, and much of the arithmetic is right. However, the total doesn't add up, the paper misdescribes its own pilot data on evening demand, and the stated pilot length conflicts with the dates given. The self-service comparison also only holds over a single year. These need correcting before the bid goes to Members.

## 1. The costs sum to £164,000, not £174,000

The three lines in Table 2 add up as follows:

£124,000 + £32,500 + £7,500 = **£164,000**

Each line checks individually:
- 5,000 h × £24.80 = £124,000
- 5 × £6,500 = £32,500

Either the total is wrong by £10,000, or a cost line is missing. The author's statement that it "all sums to £174,000" is incorrect as the table stands. If £164,000 is right, the bid can be reduced. If something has been left out, it needs to be shown.

## 2. Evening demand is not "close to daytime levels"

Table 1 shows evening visits at **21 per hour**, compared with:
- 46 per hour on weekday mornings
- 58 per hour on weekday afternoons
- about 53.5 per hour as a weighted weekday daytime average

Evening use is therefore around **40% of daytime**, not close to it. The claim appears three times: in section 3, in the conclusion, and in the author's summary. Section 3 then uses it to argue that the hours "will be well used across all five branches."

The pilot does support **Sunday** opening, at 52 per hour, close to weekday levels. The evidence for evenings is weaker. Evenings take 6 of the 10 extra hours and 60% of the staffing cost, yet produce about 38% of the extra visits. Members may reasonably ask whether all six evening hours are justified.

## 3. The pilot lasted six months, not twelve

Section 3 gives the dates as October 2025 to March 2026. The conclusion calls it "the twelve-month Ashgrove pilot." Six months is the correct figure.

A winter-only pilot also has implications:
- **Seasonal demand:** dark evenings may depress evening visits, or the weather may push people indoors. Either way, the summer pattern is untested.
- **Utilities:** these are based on winter costs "scaled to a full year," so they probably overstate heating and lighting for the summer months. That would make the estimate conservative, but the paper should say so.

## 4. The new memberships figure doesn't isolate the effect of the new hours

The 65% rise (1,140 vs 690) is correctly described as about two-thirds. But it compares the whole branch with the same period a year earlier. Without further evidence, the paper can't attribute the rise to the extra hours. It would need to show either:
- **Timing:** how many memberships were taken out during evening and Sunday sessions, or
- **Comparison:** how memberships changed at the other four branches over the same period, as a control.

A borough-wide campaign or other changes could explain part of the increase.

## 5. Ashgrove rates are applied to all five branches

The 84,000 visits figure is correctly calculated from Ashgrove's rates:
- **Per branch per week:** (6 h × 21) + (4 h × 52) = 334 visits
- **All five branches:** 334 × 50 weeks × 5 ≈ 83,500

But section 7 acknowledges that Ashgrove is the **busiest** branch and the others may be lower. The value-for-money figure ignores this, and two further points weaken it:
- **"Additional" visits:** some Sunday and evening visitors would otherwise have come at other times, so not all are new.
- **Like-for-like comparison:** the £2 figure is the *marginal* cost per visit. The £3.40 borough figure is an *average* that includes buildings, stock and management. The two aren't comparable.

A sensitivity at, say, 60% and 80% of Ashgrove's rates for the other four branches would be more realistic.

## 6. The self-service comparison only holds over one year

The author says self-service "would cost more once building works are included." Working from the paper's own figures:
- **Capital cost:** £60,000 × 5 = **£300,000**, one-off
- **Annual staffing saving:** about two-thirds of £124,000 ≈ **£83,000 a year**
- **Payback:** about **3.6 years**, after which self-service is cheaper

The comparison also mixes a one-off capital cost with a recurring revenue cost, and those usually sit in different budgets. The paper should show the multi-year comparison honestly.

A **hybrid** option isn't considered either. Under a hybrid, the Sunday sessions and the job club evening would be staffed, and the lower-demand evening hours would be self-service.

Two further points need clarifying:
- **Staffing under self-service:** if access is unstaffed, why is only two-thirds of staffing saved? The remaining third needs explaining.
- **Kiosk line:** why does a staffed option need £7,500 of self-service kiosk upgrades?

## 7. Smaller points

- **Target group not evidenced.** The rationale targets working-age adults, but the pilot gives no breakdown of evening or Sunday users by age. The families on Sundays may not be the 25–54 non-users identified in the survey.
- **Staffing rate.** One blended rate including a Sunday enhancement is used for all 5,000 hours. It would be clearer to cost evening and Sunday hours separately, since only 40% of hours are on Sundays. The paper should also confirm whether evening hours attract any enhancement.
- **Review point.** The six-month review has no criteria. The paper should say what visit level would lead to reducing or withdrawing hours at a branch.
- **Recruitment.** "As happened during the pilot" covered one branch. Five branches need about 100 extra staff hours a week, so the paper should confirm there is enough interest among existing staff.

## What holds up

- The pilot is a real strength. It tested the exact pattern and measured usage by time slot.
- Staffing arithmetic, the utilities line and the visit projection are all calculated correctly from their inputs.
- Sunday opening is well supported, at 52 visits per hour, and so is the job club.
- The rationale links clearly to the survey and the Council Plan.

## Recommended changes

1. Correct the total to £164,000, or add the missing line.
2. Describe evening demand accurately, at about 40% of daytime, and consider fewer evening hours or one late night.
3. Correct "twelve-month" to six months and note the winter-only timing.
4. Show how many new memberships came in the new hours, or compare with the other branches.
5. Model visits at the four other branches at lower rates, and drop or caveat the comparison with the borough average cost.
6. Present a multi-year self-service comparison and a hybrid option, and explain the kiosk line.
7. Set clear review criteria for continuing hours at each branch.

With these changes the bid would still be strong for Sunday opening. The evening hours would need a more modest case.
